title: PP-Mark: Provable and Publicly Verifiable Watermarking for Generative AI
claim: A two-sided protocol embeds a watermark with a verifiable proof at generation, so anyone can check both detection and proof publicly.
layout: 3 regions, left-to-right: generation, shared artifacts, verification; orange arrows trace samples
description: A wide figure split into three tinted regions. On the left, a blue 'Generation' panel starts with a payload bit string and a binding box (context hash tied to a secret key). A text prompt, 'A photo of a red apple on a wooden table', feeds a latent noise grid with orange-circled cells. Orange arrows lead to a box of deterministic samples with a trace and Merkle root, and a Denoising Diffusion trapezoid leads onward. In the center, a purple 'Publishable Artifacts' panel shows a watermarked apple image above a metadata box listing the ZKP proof properties P1 to P4. On the right, a pink 'Public Verification (no central API)' panel runs Latent Inversion into recovered latent noise and regenerated samples. A box on the far right lists watermark detection and ZKP verification steps, ending in accept = score_pass ∧ proof_ok. Private input and public artifact boxes sit at the bottom.
caption: PP-Mark overview. The generator embeds a latent watermark, commits sampled traces to a Merkle root, and produces a ZKP receipt. Verification uses latent inversion to compute a detection score and validates the receipt; acceptance requires both.
abstract: Generative AI models now produce images indistinguishable from real data, making publicly verifiable provenance essential; however, existing watermarking methods become vulnerable to forgeries and adversarial optimization attacks once their detectors are made public. We propose PP-Mark, a provenance framework that anchors lightweight statistical detection to a zero-knowledge proof of the embedding process, ensuring that forged content cannot pass full verification by construction. We establish formal unforgeability under standard cryptographic assumptions and validate PP-Mark against representative baselines across two latent-diffusion models (SD2.1 and SDXL), demonstrating resistance to black-box imprint forgery, white-box optimization, and regeneration attacks while remaining practical for decentralized verification. Code is available at https://github.com/hko920920/PP-Mark_NeurIPS2026
